newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian trucker strike prompts government threats.
newsitem.headline: Colombian trucker strike prompts government threats.

text.p: The government unveiled a series of tough measures on Wednesday aimed at ending a 10-day strike by Colombian truck drivers that has wreaked havoc on the economy.
The measures were announced by Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, who has been acting head of state since President Ernesto Samper departed on a whirlwind tour of Asia last Friday.
They included a call on the police and military to move immediately to clear all barricades erected across highways by strikers over the past week.

The government also ordered provincial governors and mayors to take any steps deemed necessary to reestablish transportation in their jurisdictions, and said authorities had been instructed to arrest anyone fostering a breakdown in law and order or the disruption of normal transport services.

Additionally, Serpa said the office of Prosecutor-General Alfonso Valdivieso had been instructed to launch an official investigation into possible "economic crimes" stemming from the work stoppage, which was declared illegal by the government last week.
Serpa also reiterated earlier threats that truckers backing the strike would have their operators' licenses revoked.

He announced the measures at a news conference after holding emergency talks early in the day with senior cabinet officials, including the finance and defence ministers, to discuss fallout from the strike that has paralysed Colombia's export industries since it began on October 13.

His news conference was called as representatives of the Colombian Truck Drivers Association (ACC) were in talks with Deputy Transportation Minister Pablo Ardila that had sparked widespread rumours about a possible peaceful settlement of the strike.
Government sources and ACC spokesmen initially said Serpa himself had joined in the talks at the Transportation Ministry, but this report was later denied.
The ACC, which represents about 90,000 drivers nationwide, called the strike to press for higher wages and lower taxes and tolls.

There was no immediate word on the outcome of Wednesday's talks, but Luz Mari Tangarife, the ACC's executive secretary, said they had been going well until Serpa announced measures aimed at ending the work stoppage by force.
"All we're hearing from the government are constant threats," Tangarife said, adding the strike would continue until the government ceded to the truckers' demands.
